```{python}
#| label: setup

from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patheffects as pe
from IPython.display import Markdown

ROOT = Path.cwd().parent if Path.cwd().name == "paper" else Path.cwd()
DATA, OUT = ROOT / "data", ROOT / "output"

HAVE_CZ = ((DATA / "PredictorLSretWide.csv").exists()
           and (DATA / "SignalDoc.csv").exists())

BLUE, ORANGE = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834"
INK, MUTED, GRID = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#d9d9d6"

mpl.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor": "white", "axes.facecolor": "white",
    "axes.edgecolor": MUTED, "axes.labelcolor": INK, "text.color": INK,
    "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED,
    "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID, "grid.linewidth": 0.6,
    "font.size": 9.5, "axes.titlesize": 10.5, "axes.titlelocation": "left",
    "legend.frameon": False, "figure.dpi": 160,
})

def ym(mi):
    """Invert mi = year*12 + month. divmod on mi - 1 keeps December in its own year."""
    y, m = divmod(int(mi) - 1, 12)
    return y, m + 1

def mi_to_ts(idx):
    return pd.to_datetime([f"{y}-{m:02d}-01" for y, m in map(ym, idx)])

HALO = [pe.withStroke(linewidth=2.6, foreground="white")]

def pct(x, d=0):
    return f"{100*x:+.{d}f}"
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

A cross-sectional return predictor is a rule: sort stocks on a characteristic, buy one
end of the sort and sell the other. Several hundred such rules have been published since
@banz1981. This paper asks what happens to one after the paper that documents it appears.

The question matters to anyone who allocates capital to a published signal. The value of
a strategy is the return it will earn from now on, net of costs, times the capital it can
carry. Publication changes that return. The recipe becomes common knowledge, capital
arrives, and the edge shrinks until what is left no longer pays for the trading it takes
to collect it [@grossman1980; @shleifer1997]. How much the edge shrinks, how fast, and
whether it stops at zero or at a floor are the three numbers an allocator needs before
deciding how much to put on a strategy and how long to keep it. We measure the first
across the whole published universe and take a step toward the second.

The word "decay" has two meanings and we use only one of them. On a trading desk, alpha
decay is the speed at which a signal's forecast loses power after it is computed. It is
measured in hours or days and it is an input to how aggressively the signal is traded
[@garleanu2013]. The decay in this paper runs on a slower clock. It is the decline in a
strategy's average monthly return over the years after the strategy becomes public. The
two share a mechanism. A short-horizon signal loses its edge within a day because other
traders act on the same information quickly; a published monthly signal loses its edge
over years because capital takes years to arrive. Below, decay always means the second.

The same logic applies to signals found by machine learning. A model fitted to past
returns is a published signal in everything but the journal. Once enough capital trades
the same features through similar models, the return the model predicts is competed
away in the same way. Published anomalies have one advantage as a laboratory: the date on
which each became common knowledge is known, so the decay can be measured against it.

What is known. @mclean2016 find, on 97 anomalies, that long-short returns are 26 percent
lower after the original sample ends and 58 percent lower after publication, and they
read the gap between those two numbers as the effect of publication itself. @chen2023
add trading costs and find that the average published anomaly earns about four basis
points a month net after 2000. @jacobs2020 find a reliable post-publication decline only
in the United States. @falck2022 find that the year of publication alone explains a
large share of how much a strategy's Sharpe ratio falls out of sample.

What this paper does. We re-measure post-publication decay on the @chen2022 universe,
which covers 212 predictors through December 2024, about twice the McLean and Pontiff
sample and a decade more data. Mean long-short returns fall 45 percent from the
original sample window to the post-publication window, and the median signal loses
53 percent. We then test the restriction that separates the two explanations of the
decline, arbitrage after publication and selection in the original sample, and we fail
to reject it: the three-window design does not identify the channel in this universe.
We rebuild two of the input series from security-level CRSP data as a check on the
dataset everything else rests on.

::: {.content-visible unless-profile="course"}
Finally we ask whether a forecaster standing in real time, knowing only the signals that
had been published by then, could have picked the ones that would keep paying. The answer
is modest. A linear regression earns an out-of-sample R² below one percent, gradient
boosted trees and a small neural network do no better, and almost all of the predictive
content sits in the signal's own return history. Holding every published signal with
equal weight earns a higher Sharpe ratio than any model-based selection.
:::

@sec-data describes the data, @sec-design the design and the estimator, @sec-result1
the results and the restriction test, @sec-rebuild the CRSP rebuild[, @sec-ml the
forecasting exercise]{.content-visible unless-profile="course"}. @sec-next sets out what
the design cannot do and what comes next.

# Data {#sec-data}

## The anomaly universe

@chen2022 reimplement several hundred published predictors from the original papers and
publish the resulting long-short portfolio return series with a documentation file that
records, for each signal, the authors, the journal, the publication year, the original
sample window and the implementation parameters. We use two files, both free:

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `PredictorLSretWide.csv` | monthly long-short returns, one column per signal |
| `SignalDoc.csv` | one row per signal: acronym, journal, `Year`, `SampleStartYear`, `SampleEndYear`, plus `Sign`, `Stock Weight`, `LS Quantile`, `Portfolio Period` |

The release is October 2025, version 2.0.0. Most series run through December 2024;
the option-implied-volatility predictors end in December 2022. This is the first release
produced by the authors' Python translation of their original Stata code, and
`ChNAnalyst`, `PriceDelayTstat` and `Recomm_ShortInterest` carry revisions from bug
fixes in that translation. All three are in the universe below.

```{python}
#| label: load
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "load the two Chen and Zimmermann files"

if not HAVE_CZ:
    raise SystemExit(
        "data/PredictorLSretWide.csv and data/SignalDoc.csv are missing.\n"
        "Both are free from https://www.openassetpricing.com (Data tab). "
        "Put them in data/ and render again."
    )

rets = pd.read_csv(DATA / "PredictorLSretWide.csv")
rets = rets.rename(columns={rets.columns[0]: "date"})
rets["date"] = pd.to_datetime(rets["date"])
doc = pd.read_csv(DATA / "SignalDoc.csv")
```

## Which signals enter

Three filters, each of which changes the answer.

1. Predictors only. The authors label some series as placebos, characteristics their own
   replication finds do not predict returns. Averaging those in would pull every window
   toward zero and flatter the decay.
2. The paper's sample must end strictly before the paper appears. Otherwise the middle
   window below is empty and the design collapses to two periods.
3. At least 24 monthly observations in every window, so that a signal cannot enter the
   post-publication average on the strength of three months.

The third filter keeps the composition fixed. The same signals appear in all three
windows, so the decline cannot come from the sample changing between them.

```{python}
#| label: panel

MIN_MONTHS = 24

d = doc[doc["Cat.Signal"] == "Predictor"].dropna(subset=["Year", "SampleEndYear"])
d = d[d["SampleEndYear"] < d["Year"]]                       # filter 2

usable = [c for c in rets.columns if c != "date" and c in set(d["Acronym"])]
long = (rets[["date"] + usable]
        .melt(id_vars="date", var_name="signal", value_name="ret")
        .dropna(subset=["ret"]))

meta = d.set_index("Acronym")[["Year", "SampleEndYear"]]
long["pub_year"] = long["signal"].map(meta["Year"]).astype(int)
long["samp_end"] = long["signal"].map(meta["SampleEndYear"]).astype(int)
long["year"] = long["date"].dt.year

long["window"] = np.select(
    [long["year"] <= long["samp_end"],
     (long["year"] > long["samp_end"]) & (long["year"] < long["pub_year"])],
    ["1_in_sample", "2_post_sample"],
    default="3_post_pub",
)
```

```{python}
#| label: matched

g = long.groupby(["signal", "window"])["ret"].agg(["mean", "size"]).unstack("window")
complete = (g["size"].fillna(0) >= MIN_MONTHS).all(axis=1)      # filter 3
table = g["mean"][complete].dropna()
table.columns = [c.split("_", 1)[1] for c in table.columns]

N_MATCHED = len(table)
N_PANEL   = long["signal"].nunique()
N_OBS     = len(long)
N_DATES   = long["date"].nunique()
```

The regression panel holds `{python} N_PANEL` signals and
`{python} f"{N_OBS:,}"` signal-months from
`{python} f"{long['date'].min():%Y-%m}"` to `{python} f"{long['date'].max():%Y-%m}"`,
across `{python} f"{N_DATES:,}"` distinct months. The matched table holds the
`{python} N_MATCHED` signals that clear all three filters.

# Design and estimator {#sec-design}

## Three windows

We cut each signal's history at two dates taken from its own paper.

| Window | Definition | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| 1. in-sample | year ≤ `SampleEndYear` | the edge as originally reported |
| 2. post-sample | `SampleEndYear` < year < `Year` | discovered, not yet public |
| 3. post-publication | year ≥ `Year` | public, and traded on |

Window 2 carries the design. If decay comes from arbitrage, nothing happens until the
paper appears: window 2 should look like window 1 and only window 3 falls. If decay comes
from selection in the original sample, window 2 is already lower, because stepping
outside the author's chosen sample is enough.

For signal $i$ let $\mu_i^{(w)}$ be its mean long-short return in window $w$. The two
estimands are

$$
\delta_1 \;=\; \mathbb{E}_i\!\left[\mu_i^{(2)} - \mu_i^{(1)}\right],
\qquad
\delta_2 \;=\; \mathbb{E}_i\!\left[\mu_i^{(3)} - \mu_i^{(1)}\right] ,
$$

and the quantity the two stories disagree about is the increment $\delta_2 - \delta_1$,
the part of the fall that arrives with publication. Arbitrage predicts
$\delta_1 \approx 0$ and $\delta_2 - \delta_1 < 0$. Pure selection predicts $\delta_1 < 0$
and $\delta_2 - \delta_1 \approx 0$.

The estimands are causal effects of publication only if the publication date is as good
as random with respect to a signal's own return path. That is not obviously true. Authors
submit when a result looks good, and journals publish with a lag that is itself related
to how strong the result is. We read the design as an event study with a pre-period.
@sec-next discusses what would tighten it.

## The regression

$$
r_{it} \;=\; \alpha_i \;+\; \beta_1 D^{\mathrm{post\text{-}sample}}_{it}
           \;+\; \beta_2 D^{\mathrm{post\text{-}pub}}_{it} \;+\; \varepsilon_{it}
$$ {#eq-main}

where $r_{it}$ is signal $i$'s long-short return in month $t$ in percent per month, the
two $D$ variables are the window indicators, and window 1 is the omitted category, so
$\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ are read against the in-sample mean. The signal fixed effect
$\alpha_i$ makes this a within comparison. Without it, $\beta_2$ would partly reflect
the fact that signals published long ago are different signals from those published
recently.

We absorb the fixed effects by subtracting each signal's own mean from every variable,

$$
\tilde z_{it} \;=\; z_{it} - \bar z_i ,
\qquad \bar z_i = \frac{1}{T_i}\sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}_i} z_{it} .
$$

By the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem [@frisch1933; @lovell1963] a regression of
$\tilde r$ on $\tilde D$ returns the same $\hat\beta$ as the regression with
`{python} N_PANEL` signal dummies. The coefficients are identified from variation over
time within a signal.

## Clustering by date

Two long-short portfolios in the same month are not independent draws. They are built
from the same stocks in the same market, and a month in which value and momentum both do
badly moves many of them together. We cluster by date, which allows arbitrary correlation
within a month. Clustering by signal would allow arbitrary correlation within a signal
over time, which is the wrong axis here [@petersen2009]. With
`{python} f"{N_DATES:,}"` months the cluster count is large enough for the asymptotics
to be reliable.

Let $g = 1,\dots,G$ index months, $\tilde X_g$ the rows of the demeaned design matrix in
month $g$ and $\hat u_g$ the residuals there. The covariance estimator is

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta)
\;=\;
c \,\bigl(\tilde X'\tilde X\bigr)^{-1}
\Bigl[\textstyle\sum_{g=1}^{G} \bigl(\tilde X_g' \hat u_g\bigr)\bigl(\tilde X_g' \hat u_g\bigr)'\Bigr]
\bigl(\tilde X'\tilde X\bigr)^{-1},
\qquad
c \;=\; \frac{G}{G-1}\cdot\frac{n-1}{n-k} .
$$ {#eq-sandwich}

Scores are summed inside a month before they are squared, so correlation within the
month is absorbed. The finite-sample factor $c$ is the usual one; it does not subtract
the absorbed fixed effects from the degrees of freedom, and with
`{python} f"{N_OBS:,}"` observations that changes the standard errors by about 0.1
percent.

```{python}
#| label: estimator

def within(df, cols, by):
    """Demean `cols` within groups of `by`. Identical to including group dummies."""
    return df[cols] - df.groupby(by)[cols].transform("mean")

def cluster_ols(y, X, cluster):
    """OLS with a cluster-robust covariance matrix, written out."""
    XtX_inv = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)
    beta    = XtX_inv @ (X.T @ y)
    u       = X * (y - X @ beta)[:, None]

    codes = pd.factorize(cluster)[0]
    G     = codes.max() + 1
    meat  = np.zeros((X.shape[1], X.shape[1]))
    for g in range(G):                       # sum scores inside a cluster, then square
        s = u[codes == g].sum(axis=0)
        meat += np.outer(s, s)

    n, k = X.shape
    c    = (G / (G - 1)) * ((n - 1) / (n - k))
    V    = c * (XtX_inv @ meat @ XtX_inv)
    return beta, V, G

def fit(sub):
    s = sub.copy()
    s["post_sample"] = (s["window"] == "2_post_sample").astype(float)
    s["post_pub"]    = (s["window"] == "3_post_pub").astype(float)
    dm = within(s, ["ret", "post_sample", "post_pub"], "signal")
    y  = dm["ret"].to_numpy()
    X  = dm[["post_sample", "post_pub"]].to_numpy()
    return cluster_ols(y, X, s["date"].to_numpy())
```

```{python}
q1, q2, q3 = (table[c].median() for c in ["in_sample", "post_sample", "post_pub"])

n_down = int((table["post_pub"] < table["in_sample"]).sum())
```

```{python}
| $\\beta_2$ post-publication | **{beta_f[1]:+.4f}** (se {se_f[1]:.4f}, **t = {beta_f[1]/se_f[1]:.2f}**) | {beta_m[1]:+.4f} (se {se_m[1]:.4f}, t = {beta_m[1]/se_m[1]:.2f}) |
| implied vs. in-sample mean | {100*beta_f[0]/abs(m1):+.0f}% and {100*beta_f[1]/abs(m1):+.0f}% | {100*beta_m[0]/abs(m1):+.0f}% and {100*beta_m[1]/abs(m1):+.0f}% |

```

@mclean2016 report about 26 percent post-sample and 58 percent post-publication over
97 anomalies. This universe is about twice as large and includes weaker and less
replicated signals. That is the first explanation for the smaller numbers and it can be
tested by re-running the design on their 97.

## What the estimates do not show

Read @tbl-panel quickly and a conclusion suggests itself: $\beta_2$ is sharply estimated
and $\beta_1$ is not, so publication is what kills the edge. That conclusion does not
survive a test.

"Publication matters over and above the end of the sample" is the restriction
$H_0: \beta_2 = \beta_1$, that is $R\beta = 0$ with $R = (-1,\;1)$. The standard error of
$R\hat\beta$ comes from the same clustered covariance matrix, and it is not the sum of
the two individual standard errors, because $\hat\beta_1$ and $\hat\beta_2$ covary:

$$
\mathrm{se}\!\left(\hat\beta_2 - \hat\beta_1\right)
= \sqrt{R \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta) R'}
= \sqrt{\widehat V_{11} + \widehat V_{22} - 2\widehat V_{12}} .
$$ {#eq-restriction}

Comparing two $t$-statistics, one significant and one not, does not test whether the
coefficients differ. @eq-restriction does.

```{python}
#| label: restriction

R = np.array([-1.0, 1.0])

def restriction(beta, V):
    diff = R @ beta
    se   = np.sqrt(R @ V @ R)
    return diff, se, diff / se

diff_f, sed_f, td_f = restriction(beta_f, V_f)
diff_m, sed_m, td_m = restriction(beta_m, V_m)
corr_f = V_f[0, 1] / np.sqrt(V_f[0, 0] * V_f[1, 1])
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-restriction
#| tbl-cap: "Testing $\\beta_2 = \\beta_1$ on the same clustered covariance."
#| echo: false

Markdown(f"""
| | $\\hat\\beta_2 - \\hat\\beta_1$, %/month | se | t |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Full panel | {diff_f:+.4f} | {sed_f:.4f} | **{td_f:.2f}** |
| Matched {N_MATCHED} | {diff_m:+.4f} | {sed_m:.4f} | {td_m:.2f} |
""")
```

The incremental effect of publication, over and above the decline that had already
happened by the time the original sample ended, is not significant at the 5 percent
level (|t| = `{python} f"{abs(td_f):.2f}"` against a critical value of 1.96). The
estimated correlation between $\hat\beta_1$ and $\hat\beta_2$ is
`{python} f"{corr_f:.2f}"`, so the difference is less precisely estimated than
$\hat\beta_2$ alone.

The point estimates are consistent with publication being the operative channel. The
data do not support that reading at conventional levels, and the three-window design
does not separate the arbitrage channel from the selection channel in this universe.
What the data do support: the post-publication decline is precisely estimated, the
post-sample decline is not, and the difference between them is too imprecise to claim.

A second limitation concerns calendar time. Publication years in this universe cluster
between the early 1990s and the mid-2010s, so for most signals "after publication" also
means "after about 2001". @chordia2014 document a decline in anomaly returns across the
board after decimalization, with growth in hedge fund assets, short interest and turnover
as the drivers. A specification with calendar-time fixed effects would separate the two,
and with staggered publication dates it is identified from the timing differences across
signals. We have not run it here; it is the first item in @sec-next.

# Rebuilding two signals from CRSP {#sec-rebuild}

Everything above is computed from return series that somebody else constructed. We
therefore rebuild two signals from security-level CRSP data and score them month by month
against the published versions: `Size`, about the simplest anomaly there is, and
`Mom12m`, which has a formation window, a skip month and overlapping holding periods and
is easy to get subtly wrong.

The pull (`03_crsp_pull.py`) and the rebuild (`04_build_anomalies.py`) need a WRDS
subscription. This section reads the committed result files and needs nothing.

## Portfolio construction

At each formation month $m$ the cross-section is sorted on the signal and cut into
$n = 1/q$ buckets, where $q$ comes from `SignalDoc`: $q = 0.5$ for `Size`, because
@banz1981 splits the market in two, and $q = 0.1$ for `Mom12m`. For a bucket $B_m$ and a
horizon $h$,

$$
\bar r^{\,B}_{m,h} \;=\;
\frac{\sum_{i \in B_m} w_{i,m}\, r_{i,\,m+h}}{\sum_{i \in B_m} w_{i,m}} ,
\qquad
\mathrm{LS}^{(h)}_{m} \;=\; s \cdot
\Bigl( \bar r^{\,\mathrm{top}}_{m,h} - \bar r^{\,\mathrm{bot}}_{m,h} \Bigr),
$$

with $w_{i,m} = 1$ for equal weighting and $w_{i,m} = \mathrm{mthcap}_{i,m}$ for value
weighting, and $s = \pm 1$ the sign from `SignalDoc`. For `Size` the sign is $-1$: the
anomaly is small minus big, and reversing it produces a significant result with the
wrong label.

`Portfolio Period` is a holding period with overlapping cohorts [@jegadeesh1993]. The
return booked in calendar month $c$ averages the cohorts formed at $c-1, \dots, c-H$,

$$
\mathrm{LS}_{c} \;=\; \frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H} \mathrm{LS}^{(h)}_{\,c-h} .
$$ {#eq-cohorts}

The momentum signal is the twelve-month return ending one month before formation,

$$
s^{\mathrm{mom}}_{i,m}
\;=\;
\exp\!\Biggl(\;\sum_{\tau = m-k-11}^{\,m-k} \log\bigl(1 + r_{i\tau}\bigr)\Biggr) - 1,
\qquad k = 1 ,
$$ {#eq-mom}

defined only where the stock has a contiguous monthly record across the window.
`Size` is $s^{\mathrm{size}}_{i,m} = \log(\mathrm{mthcap}_{i,m})$.

## The comparison

```{python}
#| label: rebuild-load
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "read the committed rebuild results"

def load_rebuild(name, col):
    df = pd.read_csv(OUT / f"rebuild_{name}.csv")
    o  = df.dropna(subset=[col, "theirs"]).copy()
    o["gap"] = o[col] - o["theirs"]
    o["year"] = [ym(v)[0] for v in o["mi"]]
    return o

reb = {"Size": load_rebuild("Size", "mine"),
       "Mom12m": load_rebuild("Mom12m", "mine_hold1")}
COL = {"Size": "mine", "Mom12m": "mine_hold1"}

def gap_t(o):
    g = o["gap"].to_numpy()
    return g.mean(), g.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(g))

def corr(o, name):
    return float(np.corrcoef(o[COL[name]], o["theirs"])[0, 1])
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-rebuild
#| tbl-cap: "Rebuilt from CRSP against the published series, on the common overlap window."
#| echo: false

rows = []
for name, conv in [("Size", "EW, halves, hold 12"), ("Mom12m", "EW, deciles, hold 1")]:
    o = reb[name]; mg, sg = gap_t(o)
    rows.append(f"| **{name}** ({conv}) | {o[COL[name]].mean():.3f} | "
                f"{o['theirs'].mean():.3f} | {mg:+.3f} (t = {mg/sg:+.2f}) | "
                f"{corr(o, name):.3f} | {len(o):,} |")

Markdown("| | rebuilt, %/month | Chen and Zimmermann | difference | corr | months |\n"
         "|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n" + "\n".join(rows))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-rebuild
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative long-short value of one dollar, log scale. Rebuilt from CRSP against the published series."
#| code-fold: true

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.6, 3.4))
for ax, name in zip(axes, ["Size", "Mom12m"]):
    o = reb[name]; x = mi_to_ts(o["mi"])
    a = (1 + o[COL[name]] / 100).cumprod().to_numpy()
    b = (1 + o["theirs"] / 100).cumprod().to_numpy()
    ax.plot(x, b, color=ORANGE, lw=1.5, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=2,
            label="Chen and Zimmermann")
    ax.plot(x, a, color=BLUE,   lw=1.1, label="rebuilt from CRSP", zorder=3)
    ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_title(name)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False); ax.margins(x=0.02)
    ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)

axes[0].set_ylabel("cumulative long-short, log scale")
axes[0].annotate("the two lines coincide", xy=(0.50, 0.08), xycoords="axes fraction",
                 fontsize=8.5, color=MUTED)
axes[1].annotate("same turning points,\nshallower slope", xy=(0.52, 0.06),
                 xycoords="axes fraction", fontsize=8.5, color=MUTED)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Size reproduces almost exactly: a difference of
`{python} f"{gap_t(reb['Size'])[0]:+.3f}"` percent a month over
`{python} f"{len(reb['Size']):,}"` months, correlation
`{python} f"{corr(reb['Size'], 'Size'):.3f}"`. In @fig-rebuild the two lines are hard to
tell apart across a century.

Momentum reproduces in shape and comes in light in level. The right-hand panel shows two
lines with the same turning points and different slopes, which on a log scale is a
roughly constant per-month shortfall.

## Is the momentum gap real?

```{python}
#| label: gap-diagnostic

o = reb["Mom12m"]
mg, sg = gap_t(o)
sd_gap = o["gap"].std(ddof=1)

# 1. thin pre-1963 data, when CRSP covers NYSE only?
pre, post = o[o["year"] < 1963], o[o["year"] >= 1963]
(mpre, spre), (mpost, spost) = gap_t(pre), gap_t(post)

# 2. a uniform implementation difference, present every month?
share_below = (o["gap"] < 0).mean()

# 3. or a tail?
worst   = o.reindex(o["gap"].abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index)
share60 = worst.head(60)["gap"].sum() / len(o) / mg
cut     = o["gap"].abs().quantile(0.90)
trim_all  = o[o["gap"].abs() <= cut]["gap"].mean()
cut_pre   = pre["gap"].abs().quantile(0.90)
trim_pre  = pre[pre["gap"].abs() <= cut_pre]["gap"].mean()
corr_abs  = float(np.corrcoef(o["gap"].abs(), o["theirs"].abs())[0, 1])
```

A momentum long-short series is volatile, and so is the month-by-month difference
between two implementations of one. The gap has a standard deviation of
`{python} f"{sd_gap:.2f}"` percent a month, so a mean of `{python} f"{mg:+.3f}"` over
`{python} f"{len(o):,}"` months carries t = `{python} f"{mg/sg:.2f}"`. Before 1963 it
is t = `{python} f"{mpre/spre:.2f}"`; from 1963 on, t = `{python} f"{mpost/spost:.2f}"`.
Neither period rejects equality.

We checked three explanations.

First, thin early data. CRSP covers NYSE only until mid-1962, so the natural guess is
that the gap sits before 1963 and the modern period replicates cleanly. It does not. The
gap is `{python} f"{mpre:+.3f}"` before 1963 and `{python} f"{mpost:+.3f}"` after.

Second, a uniform implementation difference. If a slightly different screen produced a
slightly different portfolio every month, the sign of the difference would be
persistent. The rebuilt series is below the published one in
`{python} f"{100*share_below:.1f}"` percent of months, a coin flip.

Third, a tail. The 60 months with the largest absolute gap, 5 percent of the sample,
carry `{python} f"{100*share60:.0f}"` percent of the mean difference. Trimming the
largest decile of months takes the full-sample gap to `{python} f"{trim_all:+.3f}"` and
flips the pre-1963 gap to `{python} f"{trim_pre:+.3f}"`. The absolute gap correlates
`{python} f"{corr_abs:.2f}"` with the absolute size of that month's published return.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-worst
#| tbl-cap: "The eight months that carry the momentum difference."
#| echo: false

rows = []
for _, r in worst.head(8).iterrows():
    y, m = ym(r["mi"])
    rows.append(f"| {y}-{m:02d} | {r['mine_hold1']:.2f} | {r['theirs']:.2f} | {r['gap']:+.2f} |")
Markdown("| Month | rebuilt | published | difference |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|\n"
         + "\n".join(rows))
```

```{python}
#| label: gap-ranks
#| echo: false

rk = o["gap"].abs().rank(ascending=False)
rank_of = lambda y, m: int(rk[(o["year"] == y) & (o["mi"] % 12 == m % 12)].iloc[0])
r_2008_12, r_2009_03 = rank_of(2008, 12), rank_of(2009, 3)
```

All eight fall between 1931 and 1943, in the momentum crashes and rebounds of the
Depression and the war years, when past losers surge and the extreme deciles turn over
violently [@daniel2016]. September 1939 is the rebound at the outbreak of war, and the
1932 and 1933 months are the largest momentum reversals on record. The post-war crash
months rank lower: December 2008 is `{python} r_2008_12`th by absolute gap and March 2009
is `{python} r_2009_03`th. In months like these a single imputed price, or one stock that
delists inside a holding period, moves a bucket mean by percentage points, and two
implementations of a decile sort part company. @shumway1997 is the classic statement of
how much the treatment of disappearing stocks matters.

We tried no screen variants. The remaining `{python} f"{abs(mg):.3f}"` percent a month
could be closed by searching filter combinations until the rebuilt series matched the
published one. That would be fitting the replication to its target, and it is the
behaviour this paper sets out to measure. One signal reproduces exactly; the other
reproduces to within sampling error.

## A definition error that correlation did not catch {#sec-skip}

`SignalDoc` defines `Mom12m` over "months t-12 and t-1". Month $t$ is excluded, which is
the $k = 1$ in @eq-mom. Our first implementation used $m-11,\dots,m$, which pulls
short-term reversal [@jegadeesh1990] into a momentum signal. Last month's return is
negatively autocorrelated, so including it adds an effect of the opposite sign.

```{python}
#| label: skip

# `mine` and `mine_noskip` both use the documented three-month holding period. They
# differ in one thing only: whether month t is inside the formation window.
ns = (pd.read_csv(OUT / "rebuild_Mom12m.csv")
        .dropna(subset=["mine", "mine_noskip", "theirs"]))
mean_skip   = ns["mine"].mean()
mean_noskip = ns["mine_noskip"].mean()
mean_theirs = ns["theirs"].mean()
corr_noskip = float(np.corrcoef(ns["mine_noskip"], ns["theirs"])[0, 1])
```

With everything else fixed at the documented three-month holding period, dropping the
skip takes the long-short mean from `{python} f"{mean_skip:.3f}"` to
`{python} f"{mean_noskip:.3f}"` percent a month, against a published
`{python} f"{mean_theirs:.3f}"`. Rebalanced monthly, where no cohort skips at all, the
mean fell to -0.009 percent a month: the premium disappeared.

The correlation with the published series stayed at
`{python} f"{corr_noskip:.3f}"` throughout, peaking at lag 0. Correlation confirms
that the merge and the calendar are right. It says nothing about whether the signal
definition is right, because a signal formed on the wrong window is still mostly the
same portfolio. Only the level catches this.

::: {.content-visible unless-profile="course"}

# Can a model pick the survivors in real time? {#sec-ml}

The decay in this section is the one measured above: the decline in a published
signal's monthly long-short return over the years after publication. We ask a forecasting
question about it. Standing in a given month, knowing only the signals that had been
published by then, could a forecaster have picked the ones that would pay next month,
and does a flexible model do this better than a linear one?

The question is the allocator's. A fund that trades published signals has to decide,
every month, which of them to keep. It also tests the mechanism from a different angle.
If decay is a predictable function of time since publication, a model given that clock
should use it. If the information is already in the signal's own return history, the
clock should add nothing once that history is in the model.

## Information set and panel

One row is a signal in a month; the target is that signal's long-short return next
month. A forecaster in month $t$ knows which signals have been published (publication
year strictly before the year of $t$), each published signal's documented sample window
and the characteristics of its paper, and each published signal's return history up to
$t$, including the months before the paper appeared, since a public recipe can be
backfilled. The forecaster knows nothing about signals not yet published. A signal
therefore enters the panel, for training and for testing, only in the years after its
publication year. This is the whole of the no-look-ahead rule, and it removes most of the
sample before 1995, when fewer than two dozen signals were public.

```{python}
#| label: ml-load
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "read the committed results of 05_ml_panel.py"

r2   = pd.read_csv(OUT / "ml_r2.csv", index_col=0)
dm   = pd.read_csv(OUT / "ml_dm.csv")
port = pd.read_csv(OUT / "ml_portfolio.csv", index_col=0)
port.index = pd.PeriodIndex(port.index, freq="M")
imp  = pd.read_csv(OUT / "ml_importance.csv", index_col=0)
curve = pd.read_csv(OUT / "ml_decay_curve.csv", index_col=0)
tuning = pd.read_csv(OUT / "ml_tuning.csv")

LAB = {"zero": "zero forecast", "own_mean": "own historical mean", "ols": "OLS",
       "enet": "elastic net", "gbrt": "gradient boosted trees",
       "mlp": "neural network (16 units)"}
MODELS = ["zero", "own_mean", "ols", "enet", "gbrt", "mlp"]
N_TEST = int(r2["n_test_rows"].iloc[0])

def perf(x):
    m, s = x.mean(), x.std(ddof=1)
    return m, s, (m / s) * np.sqrt(12), m / (s / np.sqrt(len(x)))

def dm_t(bench, model):
    return float(dm[(dm["benchmark"] == bench) & (dm["model"] == model)]["dm_t"].iloc[0])
```

Every model sees the same 27 features, all known at $t$:

- the signal's own history: last month's return, its mean over the past 12, 36 and 60
  months and over its whole history, and its 12-month volatility;
- event time: months since the end of the paper's sample, months since publication, and
  the two indicators that follow from them;
- the paper: publication year, length of the original sample, the $t$-statistic and
  mean return the original paper reported, the quantile cut, the holding period, whether
  the portfolio is value-weighted, whether the sort is on a discrete variable, the data
  type of the characteristic and whether the journal is one of the three top finance
  journals;
- market state, built from the panel itself: last month's equal-weighted return across
  the signals that were public, and its 12-month mean and volatility.

Nothing comes from outside the two input files.

## Models and validation

Two benchmarks fit nothing: a forecast of zero, and the signal's own historical mean
return. Against them we fit a linear regression, an elastic net, gradient boosted trees
and a neural network with one hidden layer of 16 units, all in scikit-learn
[@pedregosa2011]. The design follows @gu2020: an expanding window with one refit per
calendar year, test years 1995 to 2024; hyperparameters chosen on the last eight years
of each training sample, after which the model is refit on the whole sample; and
out-of-sample $R^2$ measured against a zero forecast. Time is kept by the target
month. A test year collects the forecasts whose target month falls in that year, every
row used to fit or tune the model for it has a target month before January of that
year, and the code checks that boundary at each refit. The out-of-sample $R^2$ is

$$
R^2_{\mathrm{oos}} \;=\; 1 - \frac{\sum_{i,t}\bigl(r_{i,t+1} - \hat r_{i,t+1}\bigr)^2}
                               {\sum_{i,t} r_{i,t+1}^{2}} .
$$

We also report $R^2$ against the own-mean benchmark, which is the harder test. The
tuning grids are small on purpose: nine settings for the elastic net, four for the trees
with the number of trees chosen on the validation sample, two for the network with
three random restarts averaged. Every setting tried is in `output/ml_tuning.csv`,
`{python} len(tuning)` rows in all. Forecast accuracy is compared with the
@diebold1995 test on the monthly average loss differential across signals, with a
@newey1987 variance at twelve lags.

## Results

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ml-r2
#| tbl-cap: "Out-of-sample R², in percent, 1995 to 2024. Columns 3 to 5 split the test rows by years since publication."
#| echo: false

rows = []
for m in MODELS:
    r = r2.loc[m]
    rows.append(f"| {LAB[m]} | {100*r['r2_vs_zero']:+.2f} | {100*r['r2_vs_own_mean']:+.2f} | "
                f"{100*r['r2_vs_zero: 0 to 3 years']:+.2f} | {100*r['r2_vs_zero: 3 to 10 years']:+.2f} | "
                f"{100*r['r2_vs_zero: over 10 years']:+.2f} |")
Markdown("| Model | vs. zero | vs. own mean | 0 to 3 years | 3 to 10 years | over 10 years |\n"
         "|----------------------------|--------:|--------:|--------:|--------:|--------:|\n"
         + "\n".join(rows))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-ml-r2
#| fig-cap: "Out-of-sample R² against a zero forecast, pooled over all test rows."
#| code-fold: true

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.3))
ms = ["own_mean", "ols", "enet", "gbrt", "mlp"]
names = ["own historical\nmean", "OLS", "elastic net", "gradient\nboosted trees",
         "neural network\n(16 units)"]
vals = [100 * r2.loc[m, "r2_vs_zero"] for m in ms]
ax.bar(names, vals, color=BLUE, width=0.6, zorder=3)
for i, v in enumerate(vals):
    ax.text(i, v + 0.02 if v >= 0 else v - 0.02, f"{v:+.2f}%", ha="center",
            va="bottom" if v >= 0 else "top", fontsize=9, color=INK)
ax.axhline(0, color=INK, lw=0.8)
ax.set_ylabel("out-of-sample R², %")
ax.set_title(f"{N_TEST:,} signal-months, test years 1995 to 2024")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)

ax.set_ylim(lo - 0.15, hi + 0.18)
fig.tight_layout()

```

Three things stand out in @tbl-ml-r2.

The numbers are small. The linear regression explains
`{python} f"{100*r2.loc['ols','r2_vs_zero']:.2f}"` percent of next month's variation,
the trees `{python} f"{100*r2.loc['gbrt','r2_vs_zero']:.2f}"` percent, and the own-mean
benchmark alone `{python} f"{100*r2.loc['own_mean','r2_vs_zero']:.2f}"` percent. This is
the order of magnitude @gu2020 report for individual stocks at the monthly horizon;
monthly long-short returns are mostly noise.

The flexible models do not beat the linear one. Against the own-mean benchmark OLS adds
`{python} f"{100*r2.loc['ols','r2_vs_own_mean']:.2f}"` percent, the trees
`{python} f"{100*r2.loc['gbrt','r2_vs_own_mean']:.2f}"` percent and the network
`{python} f"{100*r2.loc['mlp','r2_vs_own_mean']:.2f}"` percent. None of the differences
is distinguishable from zero: the Diebold-Mariano statistic for OLS against the own
mean is `{python} f"{dm_t('own_mean','ols'):+.2f}"`, for the trees against OLS
`{python} f"{dm_t('ols','gbrt'):+.2f}"`, and for the network against OLS
`{python} f"{dm_t('ols','mlp'):+.2f}"`. On this panel a model that can represent
interactions and nonlinearities finds none worth having.

Predictability does not fall with age. The $R^2$ is as high for signals more than ten
years past publication as for signals in their first three years. Whatever is
predictable about a published signal's next return is still predictable long after the
paper.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ml-imp
#| tbl-cap: "Permutation importance: the rise in pooled test mean squared error when a group of features is shuffled within each test year."
#| echo: false

rows = [f"| {g} | {r['gbrt_mse_increase']:+.4f} | {r['ols_mse_increase']:+.4f} |"
        for g, r in imp.iterrows()]
Markdown("| Feature group | gradient boosted trees | OLS |\n"
         "|------------------------------|------------------:|--------:|\n" + "\n".join(rows))
```

```{python}
#| label: ml-imp-numbers
#| echo: false

others = imp.drop(index="own history")
second_name = others["gbrt_mse_increase"].idxmax()
second_gb = others.loc[second_name, "gbrt_mse_increase"]
rest_max = others.drop(index=second_name)[["gbrt_mse_increase", "ols_mse_increase"]].abs().max().max()
```

@tbl-ml-imp says where the predictive content sits. Shuffling the signal's own return
history raises the test error by `{python} f"{imp.loc['own history','gbrt_mse_increase']:.3f}"`
for the trees and `{python} f"{imp.loc['own history','ols_mse_increase']:.3f}"` for OLS.
The next largest group for the trees is `{python} second_name`, at
`{python} f"{second_gb:.3f}"`; every other group moves the error by less than
`{python} f"{rest_max:.3f}"` in either direction, and for several of them the error
falls, which is what noise looks like under permutation. Event time in particular adds
nothing once the signal's own history is in the model.

```{python}
#| label: ml-decay-numbers
#| echo: false

raw_mean = raw["mean"].mean()
pd_ols_0, pd_ols_20 = pdp.loc[0, "pd_ols"], pdp.loc[240, "pd_ols"]
pd_gb_0, pd_gb_20 = pdp.loc[0, "pd_gbrt"], pdp.loc[240, "pd_gbrt"]
```

@fig-ml-decay puts the two readings of decay side by side. The dots are unconditional:
the average return of published signals in each year after publication, averaged across
whatever signals were in the panel. They sit around
`{python} f"{raw_mean:.2f}"` percent a month, close to the post-publication window mean
in @tbl-windows, and they show no trend over twenty years. The lines are conditional.
They show what each model predicts as the publication clock moves while the signal's
own history and everything else is held fixed. The OLS line falls from
`{python} f"{pd_ols_0:.2f}"` at publication to `{python} f"{pd_ols_20:.2f}"` twenty years
later: the monthly return drops by about
`{python} f"{abs(pd_ols_20 - pd_ols_0)/20*100:.1f}"` basis points for each year that
passes. The tree line is flat at `{python} f"{pd_gb_0:.2f}"`.

The two readings are consistent. Decay shows up in the level of the dots relative to
the in-sample mean in @tbl-windows, which is the result of @sec-result1. It does not show
up as a slope within the post-publication period, and it does not show up as a function
of the clock once the model knows the signal's recent returns. Whatever the publication
date tells a forecaster is already in the return series by the time the forecaster could
use it.

## Choosing among published signals

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ml-port
#| tbl-cap: "Portfolios formed each month from the published signals, 1995 to 2024. Monthly returns in percent; Sharpe ratios annualised."
#| echo: false

rows = []
for m in ["own_mean", "ols", "enet", "gbrt", "mlp"]:
    for leg, name in [("top", "top fifth"), ("spread", "top fifth minus bottom fifth")]:
        mean, sd, sh, t = perf(port[f"{m}_{leg}"])
        rows.append(f"| {LAB[m]}, {name} | {mean:.3f} | {sd:.3f} | {sh:.2f} | {t:.2f} |")
mean, sd, sh, t = perf(port["all"])
rows.append(f"| **all published signals, equal-weighted** | **{mean:.3f}** | **{sd:.3f}** | **{sh:.2f}** | **{t:.2f}** |")
Markdown("| Portfolio | mean | vol | Sharpe | t |\n"
         "|------------------------------------------------------|------:|------:|------:|------:|\n"

```

```{python}
#| label: fig-ml-port

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.8))
for m, color, ls in [("ols", ORANGE, (0, (4, 2))), ("gbrt", BLUE, "-"),

    ax.plot(cum.index.to_timestamp(), cum, color=color, ls=ls, lw=1.5,
            label=f"top fifth by {LAB[m]}", zorder=3)
cum = (1 + port["all"] / 100).cumprod()
ax.plot(cum.index.to_timestamp(), cum, color=INK, lw=1.3, label="all published signals",
        zorder=4)
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_ylabel("value of one dollar, log scale")
ax.set_title("Choosing among published signals")
ax.legend(fontsize=8.2, loc="upper left")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False); ax.margins(x=0.02)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: ml-port-numbers
#| echo: false

p_all = perf(port["all"]); p_own = perf(port["own_mean_top"]); p_ols = perf(port["ols_top"])
p_gb = perf(port["gbrt_top"])
```

@tbl-ml-port is the allocator's table. Holding every published signal with equal weight
earns `{python} f"{p_all[0]:.2f}"` percent a month at a volatility of
`{python} f"{p_all[1]:.2f}"`, a Sharpe ratio of `{python} f"{p_all[2]:.2f}"`. Ranking
signals by their own historical mean and holding the top fifth raises the mean to
`{python} f"{p_own[0]:.2f}"` and the Sharpe ratio to `{python} f"{p_own[2]:.2f}"`.
Ranking by the OLS forecast raises the mean further, to `{python} f"{p_ols[0]:.2f}"`,
and doubles the volatility, so the Sharpe ratio falls to `{python} f"{p_ols[2]:.2f}"`;
the trees give `{python} f"{p_gb[0]:.2f}"` and `{python} f"{p_gb[2]:.2f}"`. The
models earn their higher mean by selecting volatile signals, and a mean-squared-error
forecast of return has no reason to care about volatility. The long-short versions of
these portfolios, which also short the bottom fifth, have the same character.

Two cautions. These are portfolios of long-short portfolios and carry no trading costs;
@chen2023 show how much of a published anomaly's gross return the costs take. And the
return to "the top fifth by own mean" is the return to persistence in the cross-section
of published anomalies, which is a statement about the data, not a strategy we would
expect to survive its own publication.

## What this section does and does not show

It shows that, in real time and without look-ahead, next month's return on a published
signal is weakly predictable, that the predictability is linear and lives in the
signal's own history, and that a model with no access to the publication date would do
as well as one with it. It does not show that machine learning cannot find structure in
anomaly returns: the features here are coarse, the panel has about 48,000 test rows,
and a model given the underlying stock-level data would face a different problem. It
also does not touch the horizon a trading desk means by decay, which would need daily
or intraday portfolio returns.

:::

# What the design cannot do, and what comes next {#sec-next}

## Calendar time and staggered treatment

Publication arrives at a different date for every signal, so @eq-main is a two-way
fixed effects regression with staggered adoption. @goodmanbacon2021 shows that such an
estimator is a weighted average of all possible two-group comparisons, including
comparisons that use already-published signals as controls for later-published ones.
When the effect varies across signals or evolves over time, and decay that continues
for years after publication is an effect that evolves, those comparisons enter with the
wrong sign. @callaway2021 and @sun2021 estimate the effect using only not-yet-published
signals as controls, and the same estimators absorb the calendar-time decline discussed
in @sec-result1. This is the next thing to build, and it should change the number.

Regression discontinuity does not apply. It needs a running variable with a cutoff and
units that cannot manipulate their position around it. Here the running variable would
be calendar time, the cutoff is anticipated, since working papers circulate for years
before a journal issue appears, and authors have some control over timing. Anticipation
alone pushes part of the decay before the event and biases the estimate toward zero, so
the post-publication decline measured here is a lower bound on the true one.

## How fast, and to what floor

A three-window average says the edge fell. It does not say how quickly, or whether it
fell to zero. The simple route fits

$$
\alpha_t \;=\; \phi + (\alpha_0 - \phi)\,e^{-\lambda t}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\text{half-life} \;=\; \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}
$$

per signal, with $\phi$ the floor. @grossman1980 says the floor should be positive, so
estimating it tests that prediction. The better route is a state-space model,

$$
r_t = \alpha_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad
\alpha_t = \phi_i + \rho_i(\alpha_{t-1} - \phi_i) + \eta_t ,
$$

estimated by the Kalman filter and maximum likelihood [@durbin2012], which returns the
floor and the half-life $\ln 2 / (-\ln \rho_i)$ with standard errors from one
estimation.

## Who dies fast

The cross-section is where the arbitrage story becomes testable: decay should be faster
where arbitrage is cheaper and where more capital has arrived. Illiquidity, market
capitalisation, idiosyncratic volatility, short interest and institutional ownership are
all computable from the CRSP panel built for @sec-rebuild. The Jensen, Kelly and Pedersen
global factor data would turn the same hypothesis into a cross-country test, and
@jacobs2020 suggest what to expect.

## Open items

- Re-run on the @mclean2016 97 to see whether the weaker channel separation is a
  composition effect.
- Replace @eq-main with the @callaway2021 and @sun2021 estimators and report how much
  the estimate moves.
- Gross profitability as a third rebuilt signal; it needs Compustat and the CCM link.

```bash
# The decay results need only the two free Chen and Zimmermann files in data/
```
